short: A number typed straight into a spreadsheet cell instead of being calculated by a formula or linked to a labelled input cell.
kid: If you write the answer to a sum without showing how you got it, nobody can check it. And if one number changes, your answer will not fix itself.
detail: A hardcode is a fixed value entered directly into a cell, or buried inside a formula such as =B5*1.08, rather than pulled from a clearly labelled input cell. Hardcodes are fine for raw historical data and for assumptions kept in a dedicated inputs section, which by convention are shown in blue. The danger lies in hidden constants inside calculation cells, or numbers pasted over formulas to force a result. When an assumption changes, the buried number does not update, so errors flow quietly into valuations, budgets and board decks. Reviewers in banks and audit teams hunt for them with Excel's Go To Special (Constants) and formula auditing tools. Common confusion: not every typed number is a mistake. The rule is that each assumption is entered once, in one visible place, with its source noted.
example: Say a model grows revenue with =B5*1.08, with the 8% growth typed inside the formula. If B5 holds FY26 revenue of ₹500 crore, FY27 shows ₹540 crore. If the growth assumption is cut to 6%, every cell with the buried 1.08 must be found and edited by hand; with a linked input cell, changing one cell instantly gives ₹530 crore.

short: Shared rules for how a spreadsheet model looks, such as blue text for typed inputs and black for formulas, so anyone can follow it.
kid: When you tidy toys, red boxes might hold cars and blue boxes hold blocks. Then anyone can find things without asking you.
detail: Model formatting conventions are the house style analysts follow so a financial model can be read and checked quickly. The most common colour code is blue font for hard-coded inputs and historical data, black for formulas calculated on the same sheet, and green for links to other sheets, with red often used for links to other files. Other habits include one consistent formula across each row, a timeline running left to right, units in every row label (₹ crore, %), negatives in brackets, shaded cells for key assumptions, and separate input, calculation and output sections. This matters because models in investment banking, equity research and FP&A pass through many hands, and a consistent style lets a reviewer spot an error or a stray hardcode in seconds. Common confusion: conventions differ slightly between firms, so follow your team's guide, but never mix styles within one model.
example: In a model of, say, ABC Ltd, FY26 revenue of ₹1,200 crore and the 10% growth assumption are typed in blue. The FY27 revenue formula, which returns ₹1,320 crore (₹1,200 crore x 1.10), is in black, and a cell pulling the tax rate from a separate assumptions sheet is in green.

short: A period shorter than a full year or quarter, used in a model when a deal or valuation date falls partway through a year.
kid: If you join a game halfway through, you only count the points from the part you played. That short bit is its own little piece.
detail: A stub period is a fraction of a financial year that a model treats on its own. It appears when a valuation date, deal closing or first reporting date does not line up with a company's year-end. In a DCF dated 1 October for a company with a 31 March year-end, only six months of the current year remain, so the analyst includes half of that year's free cash flow and shifts every later discount period by the same half year. In LBO and merger models, the stub runs from closing to the first full year-end. Companies also report stub periods when they change their financial year, as many Indian companies did after the Companies Act, 2013 required most of them to end their year on 31 March. Common confusion: adjusting the cash flow but forgetting to adjust the discount periods, which overstates value.
example: Say a DCF of ABC Ltd is dated 1 October 2025 and FY26 (April 2025 to March 2026) free cash flow is forecast at ₹200 crore. Only six months remain, so the stub cash flow is ₹200 crore x 6/12 = ₹100 crore. Assuming cash arrives at each year-end, it is discounted for 0.5 years, and FY27's cash flow for 1.5 years rather than 2.
formula: Stub-period cash flow = Full-year cash flow x (Months remaining / 12); first discount period = Months remaining / 12

short: Adjusting a company's figures from its own financial year to a common twelve-month period so companies with different year-ends can be compared.
kid: One friend counts birthday presents from January, another from April. To be fair, you count both from the same day before comparing.
detail: Calendarisation restates financial data so that every company in a comparison covers the same twelve months. It is essential when spreading comparable companies: most Indian listed firms report on an April to March financial year, many global peers use January to December, and some retailers use other year-ends. Comparing one peer's multiple on a March year with another's on a December year mixes different periods and distorts the result, especially for fast-growing or cyclical businesses. The usual method weights two fiscal years by the number of months each contributes to the target period; when quarterly data is available, adding the four relevant quarters is more accurate, particularly for seasonal businesses. Common confusion: calendarisation does not always mean converting to January to December. It means aligning everyone to one chosen period, often the year-end of the buyer or of most peers.
example: Say ABC Ltd's year ends on 31 March, with EBITDA of ₹400 crore in FY25 (April 2024 to March 2025) and ₹480 crore in FY26. Calendar 2025 takes 3 months from FY25 and 9 months from FY26: 0.25 x 400 + 0.75 x 480 = 100 + 360 = ₹460 crore.
formula: Calendarised figure = (m / 12) x Fiscal year 1 figure + ((12 - m) / 12) x Fiscal year 2 figure, where m = months of the target period falling in fiscal year 1

short: Collecting and standardising financial data for a group of similar companies in a spreadsheet so their valuation multiples can be compared fairly.
kid: To know a fair price for your bike, you look at what similar bikes sold for. First you check they are the same size and age, so the comparison is fair.
detail: Spreading comps is the hands-on work behind comparable company analysis. An analyst chooses a peer group, then pulls revenue, EBITDA, net income, net debt, share count and share price from annual reports, quarterly results and data terminals into a standard template. The crucial step is normalising: removing one-off items such as exceptional gains or restructuring costs, using diluted share counts, calendarising to a common period, converting currencies and making sure EBITDA is defined the same way for everyone, for example before or after lease costs under Ind AS 116 and IFRS 16. The output is a table of multiples such as EV/EBITDA and P/E, with medians and means used to value the target. It is a core task for junior analysts in investment banking and equity research. Common confusion: copying numbers straight from a screener gives multiples that look precise but compare unlike things.
example: Say peer A has an enterprise value of ₹6,000 crore and reported EBITDA of ₹600 crore, including a one-off ₹100 crore gain on selling land. Unadjusted, its EV/EBITDA is 10.0x; after removing the gain, EBITDA is ₹500 crore and the multiple is 12.0x, which is the figure that belongs in the comps table.
formula: Trading multiple = Enterprise value (or market capitalisation) / Normalised financial metric

short: A spreadsheet that tests a buyout funded mostly with borrowed money, showing how debt is repaid and what return the buyer earns on exit.
kid: You borrow most of the coins from your big brother to buy a lemonade stand, then pay him back bit by bit from the lemonade you sell. Later you sell the stand and see how much your own few coins grew.
detail: An LBO model projects a leveraged buyout, in which a private equity sponsor buys a company using a large amount of debt and a smaller equity cheque. It starts with the purchase price and a sources and uses table, builds the target's operating forecast, and then a debt schedule in which free cash flow pays interest and repays loans year by year. At exit, typically three to seven years later, it assumes a sale at an exit multiple, subtracts remaining net debt, and calculates the sponsor's IRR and multiple of money (MOIC). Returns come from three levers: EBITDA growth, debt paydown and a higher exit multiple. Common confusion: the model does not show what the business is worth to every buyer; it shows the most a sponsor can pay while still reaching its target return, often 20% or more.
example: Say a fund buys ABC Ltd for ₹1,000 crore using ₹600 crore of debt and ₹400 crore of equity. Over five years it repays ₹300 crore of debt and then sells the company for ₹1,300 crore. Equity at exit is ₹1,300 crore - ₹300 crore of remaining debt = ₹1,000 crore, a 2.5x multiple of money, or an IRR of about 20% a year.
formula: MOIC = Equity value at exit / Equity invested; IRR = MOIC^(1 / years held) - 1 (when there are no interim cash flows)

short: A quick, simplified sum of a debt-funded buyout's returns, done by hand or mentally, often set in private equity interviews.
kid: Before building a big sandcastle, you scratch a quick plan in the sand with a stick. It is rough, but it tells you whether the idea can work.
detail: A paper LBO strips a full LBO model down to its essentials so it can be solved with pen and paper in about 10 to 15 minutes. The candidate is given entry EBITDA, an entry multiple, the debt level, growth, margins and exit assumptions, and must work out the purchase price, the debt and equity split, the free cash flow used to repay debt, the exit equity value, and the resulting multiple of money and approximate IRR. Simplifications are standard: round numbers, no fees, all free cash flow repaying debt, and rules of thumb such as doubling money in five years being roughly a 15% IRR and tripling it in five years roughly 25%. Private equity firms use it to test whether a candidate understands what drives returns, not spreadsheet speed. Common confusion: precision is not the point; a sound structure and sensible rounding matter more than the exact decimal.
example: Buy a company with EBITDA of $100 million at 10x, so the price is $1,000 million, funded with $600 million of debt and $400 million of equity. If EBITDA grows to $120 million, the exit is also at 10x ($1,200 million) and $200 million of debt is repaid over five years, exit equity is $1,200 million - $400 million = $800 million: a 2.0x return, or roughly 15% a year.
formula: Exit equity = Exit EBITDA x Exit multiple - Net debt at exit; MOIC = Exit equity / Entry equity

short: A table showing where a deal's money comes from and how it is spent; the two sides must add up to the same total.
kid: Money for a class party comes from what each friend brings and what the teacher adds. You list that on one side, what you spend on cake and balloons on the other, and both sides must match.
detail: A sources and uses table summarises how a transaction such as an acquisition, LBO or project is funded. Uses list everything the money is needed for: buying the target's equity, refinancing its existing debt, paying fees, and sometimes cash left on the balance sheet. Sources list where it comes from: new loans or bonds, the buyer's or sponsor's equity, equity rolled over by sellers, and existing cash. Because every rupee raised must be spent, total sources must equal total uses; in an LBO model, sponsor equity is often the balancing figure. It is usually the first schedule bankers build. In an Indian IPO prospectus, the section on the objects of the issue plays a similar role for the money raised. Common confusion: the equity purchase price is not the only use; refinanced debt and fees can add a lot to the cash needed.
example: Say a fund buys ABC Ltd's equity for ₹800 crore, refinances its ₹150 crore of existing debt and pays ₹50 crore in fees, so uses total ₹1,000 crore. It funds this with ₹550 crore of new term loans and ₹450 crore of its own equity, so sources also total ₹1,000 crore.

short: A spreadsheet that combines a buyer's and a target's forecasts to show whether an acquisition raises or lowers the buyer's earnings per share.
kid: You pour your sweets together with a friend's, but more people now share the bowl. You check whether each person's handful gets bigger or smaller.
detail: A merger model, or accretion-dilution model, estimates how an acquisition changes the buyer's financials. It takes the purchase price and how it is paid for (cash, new debt or new shares), adds the target's net income to the buyer's, subtracts lost interest on cash used, new interest on debt raised and extra amortisation from the purchase price allocation, adds expected synergies, and divides by the new share count. If pro forma EPS is higher than the buyer's standalone EPS, the deal is accretive; if lower, dilutive. A quick test for an all-stock deal: it is accretive when the buyer's P/E is higher than the P/E it pays for the target. Bankers also check leverage and ownership after the deal. Common confusion: accretion does not mean the deal creates value; a buyer can overpay and still lift EPS if it funds the deal with cheap debt.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹100 crore on 10 crore shares (EPS ₹10) and buys XYZ Ltd, which earns ₹20 crore, by issuing 1.5 crore new shares. Pro forma EPS = (100 + 20) / 11.5 = ₹10.43, about 4.3% higher, so the deal is accretive before synergies and costs.
formula: Pro forma EPS = (Buyer net income + Target net income + After-tax synergies - After-tax financing and amortisation costs) / (Buyer shares + New shares issued)

short: An Excel function that values future payments falling on uneven dates in today's money, using the exact number of days until each one.
kid: A sweet you get today is worth more to you than one promised much later. This tool counts the exact days you must wait for each sweet.
detail: XNPV(rate, values, dates) calculates net present value when cash flows do not arrive at evenly spaced intervals. Each cash flow is discounted by (1 + rate) raised to the number of days since the first date divided by 365. The ordinary NPV function assumes equal periods and treats its first value as arriving one period from now, so users often wrongly discount the initial investment. XNPV discounts everything back to the first date in the range, so the first cash flow is not discounted at all. It is the usual choice for DCFs with stub periods and for project finance and private equity cash flows. Points to watch: the rate is annual, dates must be real Excel dates, and if the valuation date differs from the first cash flow date, add a zero cash flow on the valuation date. XIRR finds the rate that makes XNPV zero.
example: An investment of ₹10 lakh on 1 April 2025 returns ₹6 lakh on 1 October 2025 (183 days later) and ₹5.5 lakh on 1 April 2026 (365 days later). At 10%, XNPV = -10 + 6 / 1.10^(183/365) + 5.5 / 1.10 = -10 + 5.72 + 5.00 = ₹0.72 lakh.
formula: XNPV = sum of CFi / (1 + r)^((di - d1) / 365), where di is the date of cash flow i and d1 is the first date

short: An Excel function giving the yearly return on cash flows that happen on irregular dates, such as monthly investments and a final withdrawal.
kid: You drop coins into a jar on different days, and later the jar holds more than you put in. This tells you how fast your coins grew each year, counting when each coin went in.
detail: XIRR(values, dates, [guess]) returns the annualised internal rate of return for cash flows on specific dates: the rate at which their XNPV equals zero. Money paid out is entered as negative and money received as positive. Unlike IRR, which assumes equally spaced periods, XIRR uses the actual days between cash flows, so it is the right measure for SIPs, top-ups, partial withdrawals and private equity distributions. Indian mutual fund statements and investment apps report XIRR for SIP portfolios because a simple absolute return or CAGR ignores that each instalment was invested for a different length of time. Common confusions: XIRR is annualised, so very short holding periods can show extreme figures; and it reflects the investor's own timing, so two people in the same fund can have different XIRRs. Like IRR, it can fail or give several answers when cash flows change sign repeatedly.
example: You invest ₹10,000 on 1 January 2025 and get back ₹11,000 on 1 January 2026, so XIRR is 10%. If instead you invest ₹10,000 on 1 January 2025 and another ₹10,000 on 1 July 2025, and the total is worth ₹21,000 on 1 January 2026, XIRR is about 6.7%, higher than the 5% simple gain, because the second ₹10,000 was invested for only half a year.
formula: XIRR is the rate r that solves: 0 = sum of CFi / (1 + r)^((di - d1) / 365), where di is the date of cash flow i and d1 is the first date

short: An Excel function that works out the fixed payment each period needed to repay a loan, interest included, over a set number of periods.
kid: You borrow some toy money from your big sister and promise to give back the same small amount every week until it is all paid. This works out how big each weekly amount must be.
detail: PMT(rate, nper, pv, [fv], [type]) returns the constant payment per period for a loan or savings plan with a fixed interest rate. Rate is the interest rate per period, nper the number of periods, pv the amount borrowed today, fv an optional balance left at the end, and type 0 for payments at the end of each period (the default) or 1 for the start. It is how EMIs on home, car and education loans are calculated: for monthly payments, divide the annual rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12. Excel uses a cash-flow sign convention, so a positive loan amount returns a negative payment; enter pv as a negative number to show the payment as positive. The related IPMT and PPMT functions split each payment into interest and principal for an amortisation schedule. Common confusion: using an annual rate with monthly periods, which grossly overstates the payment.
example: A ₹10 lakh loan at 12% a year, repaid monthly over one year: =PMT(12%/12, 12, -1000000) gives an EMI of about ₹88,849. Twelve such payments total about ₹10.66 lakh, so roughly ₹66,000 of the total is interest.
formula: PMT = PV x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n), where r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods

short: An Excel function that finds an item in a table's first column and returns a value from another column in that row.
kid: You run your finger down a list of names to find your friend, then slide it across to see their phone number. This does the finding and sliding for you.
detail: VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]) searches down the leftmost column of a range and returns the item from a chosen column number in the same row. Its sibling HLOOKUP searches across the top row and returns from a row below. In finance it pulls a company's sector into a comps sheet or maps ledger codes to report lines. Pitfalls: the last argument defaults to approximate match, so leaving out FALSE (or 0) on an unsorted list can silently return the wrong row; it cannot return values to the left of the lookup column; the typed column number breaks when columns are inserted; and it returns only the first match. Because of these limits, many analysts prefer INDEX-MATCH or, in newer Excel versions, XLOOKUP. Common confusion: a #N/A error usually means no exact match was found, often because of extra spaces or numbers stored as text.
example: A table in A2:C4 lists tickers in column A, sectors in column B and prices in column C: say ABC at ₹250, DEF at ₹410 and GHI at ₹95. If E1 holds DEF, =VLOOKUP(E1, A2:C4, 3, FALSE) returns ₹410, the price in the third column of the row where DEF appears.
formula: =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, FALSE) for an exact match

short: A newer Excel function that finds an item in one list and returns the matching item from another list, looking in any direction.
kid: You find your friend's name on one list, then look at a second list to see their favourite colour, whichever side that list is on.
detail: XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]) arrived in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 as a successor to VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP. Instead of a column number, you point to separate lookup and return ranges, so it can return values to the left, keeps working when columns are inserted, and works vertically or horizontally. It uses exact match by default, lets you set a fallback value instead of a #N/A error, can search from the bottom up to find the latest entry, and can return several adjacent columns at once. In financial models this makes lookups of tickers, account codes or scenario assumptions sturdier and easier to audit. Common confusion: XLOOKUP does not exist in Excel 2016 or 2019, so a model opened in those versions shows #NAME? errors; that is why many banks still use INDEX-MATCH for compatibility.
example: With tickers ABC, DEF and GHI in A2:A4 and prices of ₹250, ₹410 and ₹95 in C2:C4, =XLOOKUP(E1, A2:A4, C2:C4, 0) returns ₹95 when E1 holds GHI, and returns 0 instead of an error when E1 holds a ticker that is not on the list.

short: Two Excel functions combined: MATCH finds an item's position in a list, and INDEX returns the value at that position in another list.
kid: First you count which seat your friend is sitting in, say seat three. Then you go to seat three in the next row to see which toy is there.
detail: INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0)) is the classic flexible lookup. MATCH with a final argument of 0 returns the position of an exact match; INDEX then returns the value at that position from any other range of the same size. Because the lookup and return ranges are separate, it can look left, does not break when columns are inserted, and is efficient on large sheets. A two-way version, INDEX(table, MATCH(row item), MATCH(column header)), picks a value by both row and column, which is handy for pulling one company's metric for one year from a comps grid or switching between base, upside and downside scenarios. It works in every Excel version, which is why banks and consulting firms still teach it alongside XLOOKUP. Common confusion: leaving out the 0 in MATCH turns it into an approximate match that needs sorted data and can silently return wrong results.
example: With tickers ABC, DEF and GHI in A2:A4 and prices of ₹250, ₹410 and ₹95 in C2:C4, if E1 holds GHI then =MATCH(E1, A2:A4, 0) returns 3 and =INDEX(C2:C4, 3) returns ₹95. Combined, =INDEX(C2:C4, MATCH(E1, A2:A4, 0)) gives ₹95 in one step.

short: An Excel function that adds up only the numbers in a list that meet one or more conditions, such as a region and a month.
kid: You have a big bag of sweets, and you count only the ones that are red and round. Everything else stays in the bag.
detail: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...) adds the cells in sum_range whose rows meet every condition given. SUMIF is the single-condition version, with its arguments in a different order (range, criteria, [sum_range]), a frequent source of errors. COUNTIFS counts the matching rows instead of adding them, and AVERAGEIFS averages them. In finance these functions turn raw transaction data into model-ready numbers: sales by product and quarter, expenses by cost centre, or the number of invoices more than 90 days overdue in a receivables ageing report. Conditions can be numbers, text, cell references or comparisons such as greater than 90. Because the result updates as data is added, SUMIFS is often preferred to manual filtering or pivot tables inside a live model. Common confusion: SUMIFS applies AND logic across its conditions; for OR logic between values that cannot overlap, such as two regions, you add two SUMIFS together.
example: A sales sheet has regions in column A, months in column B and sales in column C. With F1 holding North and G1 holding Apr-25, =SUMIFS(C2:C500, A2:A500, F1, B2:B500, G1) adds only North's April sales; if the matching rows hold ₹12 lakh, ₹8 lakh and ₹5 lakh, the result is ₹25 lakh.

short: An Excel tool that summarises a large table of data into totals, counts or averages by category, rearranged with drag and drop.
kid: You tip out a huge box of toys and sort them into piles: cars here, dolls there, blocks over there. Then you count each pile in a flash.
detail: A pivot table takes a flat dataset, where each row is one record such as an invoice or a trade, and summarises it by the fields you choose for rows, columns, values and filters. Dragging Region into rows and Revenue into values instantly totals revenue by region; adding Quarter to columns turns it into a region-by-quarter grid. Values can be shown as sums, counts, averages or percentages of the total, and slicers make filtering easy. Analysts use them to explore data before modelling, such as sales by product or expenses by department. In India, FP&A and audit teams often use them to summarise data exported from accounting and ERP systems such as Tally or SAP. Common confusions: a pivot table does not update by itself when the source data changes, so you must refresh it; and linking model formulas to pivot cells is fragile, so GETPIVOTDATA or SUMIFS is safer.
example: Say a sheet lists 10,000 invoices of ABC Ltd. A pivot table with Region in rows and Amount in values shows North at ₹40 crore, South at ₹35 crore and West at ₹25 crore; switching the display to percentage of grand total shows 40%, 35% and 25% of the ₹100 crore total.

short: A cell address locked with dollar signs, like $B$2, so it keeps pointing at the same cell when a formula is copied elsewhere.
kid: When you move along a row of chairs, what you see changes too. But if you keep your eyes fixed on the teacher, you look at the same spot wherever you sit.
detail: Excel formulas use relative references by default: a formula containing B2, copied one column to the right, becomes C2. An absolute reference, written $B$2, keeps both column and row fixed wherever the formula is copied. Mixed references lock only one part: $B2 fixes the column and B$2 fixes the row. Pressing F4 on Windows (Fn+F4 on many laptops) or Cmd+T on a Mac cycles through the four options. Anchoring is essential in models: a growth or tax rate stored in one input cell must be referenced absolutely so every year's formula points to it, and a sensitivity grid uses mixed references so one formula fills both rows and columns. Common confusions: the dollar sign has nothing to do with currency; and forgetting to anchor is one of the most frequent spreadsheet errors, because the copied formulas still return plausible-looking numbers while pointing at the wrong, often blank, cells.
example: An assumed tax rate of 25% sits in B1, and pre-tax profits of ₹40 lakh, ₹50 lakh and ₹60 lakh sit in C3:E3. Typing =C3*$B$1 in C4 and copying it right gives ₹10 lakh, ₹12.5 lakh and ₹15 lakh. Without the dollar signs, the copied formulas would point to C1 and D1 instead of B1 and give wrong results.

short: Comparing actual results with the budget or forecast, measuring each gap, and explaining why it happened.
kid: You planned to sell ten cups of lemonade but sold only seven. You look at the difference and think about why; maybe it rained.
detail: Variance analysis measures the gap between actual figures and a benchmark, usually the budget, a reforecast or the prior year, and explains what caused it. Each variance is labelled favourable when it helps profit (revenue above plan, costs below plan) and unfavourable when it hurts. Analysts then break variances into drivers: revenue into price, volume and mix effects, and costs into rate and usage effects. It is the core monthly and quarterly routine of FP&A and management accounting teams, feeding management reviews and board packs, and it prompts action such as cutting discretionary spending or revising the forecast. Investors run a similar exercise when quarterly results beat or miss consensus estimates. Common confusions: a cost that comes in higher than budget is unfavourable even though the number went up, so sign conventions must be stated clearly; and the statistical variance, a measure of spread, is unrelated.
example: Say ABC Ltd budgeted to sell 10,000 units at ₹500 (₹50 lakh) but sold 9,000 units at ₹520 (₹46.8 lakh). The ₹3.2 lakh unfavourable revenue variance splits into a volume effect of -1,000 x ₹500 = -₹5 lakh and a price effect of +₹20 x 9,000 = +₹1.8 lakh.
formula: Variance = Actual - Budget; Price variance = (Actual price - Budget price) x Actual volume; Volume variance = (Actual volume - Budget volume) x Budget price

short: The finance team inside a company that builds budgets and forecasts, tracks performance against them, and advises leaders on decisions.
kid: Before a school fair, someone plans how many cookies to bake and sell. Afterwards they check what really happened and help plan better next time.
detail: Financial planning and analysis (FP&A) is the forward-looking side of a company's finance function, distinct from accounting, which records what has happened, and treasury, which manages cash and funding. FP&A runs the annual budget and operating plan, prepares rolling forecasts, builds driver-based models of revenue and costs, performs monthly variance analysis, and evaluates decisions such as price changes, new plants or hiring plans. It produces management dashboards and board packs and often owns key metrics such as margins and unit economics. In India, large business groups, consumer companies and the global capability centres (GCCs) of multinationals run sizeable FP&A teams, making it a common entry point into corporate finance careers. Common confusion: FP&A is not financial reporting; its outputs are internal and rely on judgement, whereas reported financial statements follow accounting standards and are audited.
example: Say ABC Ltd's FP&A team budgets FY27 revenue at ₹1,000 crore, with ₹500 crore planned for the first half. Actual first-half revenue is ₹460 crore, an 8% shortfall, so the team traces it to weak volumes in one region and cuts the full-year forecast to ₹950 crore.

short: Forecasting a company's revenue by multiplying its underlying drivers, such as units sold and price per unit, rather than guessing one growth rate.
kid: To guess how many coins your lemonade stand will make, you think about how many cups you will sell and the price of each cup, then multiply.
detail: A revenue build forecasts the top line from its operating drivers instead of applying one growth rate to last year's sales. Typical builds are volume x price (tonnes x realisation per tonne for a cement maker), stores x revenue per store for a retailer, subscribers x average revenue per user for a telecom company, loan book x yield for a lender, and rooms x occupancy x average room rate for a hotel. Builds can be bottom-up, starting from units, customers or capacity, or top-down, starting from market size x market share. Because revenue drives almost every other line of a three-statement model, a well-grounded build makes the forecast explainable and lets analysts test each assumption separately. A revenue bridge applies the same logic backwards, splitting the change between two periods into price, volume and mix. Common confusion: more detail is not automatically more accuracy; every driver needs evidence.
example: Say ABC Cements Ltd expects to sell 50 lakh tonnes in FY27 at ₹5,000 a tonne, so its revenue build gives 50 lakh x ₹5,000 = ₹2,500 crore. If volume rises 10% and price falls 2%, revenue becomes 55 lakh x ₹4,900 = ₹2,695 crore.
formula: Revenue = Volume x Price per unit (or Customers x Average revenue per customer)

short: A chart that starts from one total, shows each increase or decrease as a floating bar, and ends at a new total, explaining the change.
kid: You start the day with ten marbles. You draw a step up when you win some and a step down when you lose some, until you reach what you have at bedtime.
detail: A waterfall chart, also called a bridge, shows how an opening value becomes a closing value through a series of positive and negative contributions. The first and last bars stand on the axis, while the bars in between float, usually green for increases and red for decreases. In finance the classic use is an EBITDA or profit bridge from last year to this year (volume, price, raw material costs, employee costs), a budget-to-actual bridge in variance analysis, or a bridge from enterprise value to equity value. Excel 2016 and later include a built-in waterfall chart type. It is a staple of management presentations and banking decks because it makes the biggest drivers obvious at a glance. Common confusions: the chart only explains the change if the steps add up exactly to the difference; and it is unrelated to a private equity distribution waterfall, which sets how fund profits are split.
example: Say ABC Ltd's EBITDA rose from ₹100 crore in FY25 to ₹120 crore in FY26. The bridge shows ₹100 crore, then +₹30 crore from higher volumes, +₹10 crore from price increases, -₹15 crore from costlier raw materials and -₹5 crore from higher salaries, ending at ₹120 crore.
formula: Closing value = Opening value + Sum of increases - Sum of decreases
